title: Frankenstein
synopsis: Ingolstadt. You are a brilliant student. You have figured out, alone in a garret, how to give life. You have not figured out what to do with what you make.

nodes.text: The hands came from a dissecting room and a slaughterhouse both, and you have stitched them at the wrist with waxed thread, forty-one passes to each joint. Eight feet of him on the table, because the small parts were too fine for your fingers. Rain starts against the garret glass. You have not eaten since Tuesday. The storm is arriving exactly on schedule, which feels like permission.

choices.consequence: You light the second candle off the stub of the first. Below you the landlady's clock strikes one, and you do not hear a single stroke of it.
You set the needle down for a full minute and think about your father's handwriting. Then you pick it up again, because you were always going to.

nodes.text: The eye opens. Yellow, watery, and it finds you at once — there is nothing newborn in how it finds you. The lips work around air they have never held. One hand lifts off the table toward you, slow, the way a child reaches up to be carried. You spent two years choosing those features for beauty. Awake, they are only skin laid over teeth.

choices.consequence: You stay in the doorway long enough to watch him try a sound that might be your name. You decline to answer to it.
You go down two flights and out into the rain in your shirtsleeves, and walk the courtyard until dawn, watching your own window for a shape at it.

nodes.text: Henry finds you folded on the stairs and carries you up like laundry. Five weeks you sweat through his sheets and argue with the corners of the room. He spoons broth, opens your post, writes to your father that it is only overwork. When the fever finally breaks he says, gently, that the garret was empty when he got there. Then he asks what you had been building.

choices.consequence: You start the sentence three separate times. What comes out is a lecture on galvanism, and Henry nods along, relieved to have his friend making sense.
You tell him chemistry, badly ventilated. He believes it instantly, and that is the moment you learn how easy the rest of this will be.

nodes.text: Your father's hand stays steady for four lines and then stops being steady. William, five years old, found in the woods at Plainpalais with the print of fingers on his throat. The locket he wore is missing. It turns up in Justine's apron pocket, exactly where Geneva expects a servant girl to keep a stolen thing. You read the date twice. Then you do the arithmetic.

choices.consequence: You testify to her character in a courtroom that has already decided it wants a witch, and say nothing whatever about the eight-foot reason you know she is innocent.
You sit in the gallery with your hat in your lap and let the girl who taught William to skip be the story instead of you.

nodes.text: She confesses to the priest, because confession is the only road to absolution and she wants absolution more than she wants to live. Then the rope, which takes some minutes. Your mother brought Justine into that house at twelve; she darned your stockings; she is the second person from your kitchen to die of you. Walking back, Elizabeth says the world is monstrous. You agree with her.

choices.consequence: You get as far as the study door, hear your father weeping on the other side of it, and turn around with the whole truth still folded up in your mouth.
You keep a decent face at supper and pass the bread when asked. Something in you goes quiet that evening and never switches back on.

nodes.text: He crosses the ice faster than a man can, half a mile in the time it takes you to draw the pistol and think better of firing. Close up, he is your own handwriting made flesh: the wrist you were proud of, the jaw you copied off an anatomy plate. He asks you to sit down. His French is better than yours. He mentions that he has been reading.

choices.consequence: You sit on a boulder in the cold with your own creation and hear him out for hours, and hating him gets measurably harder with every sentence.
You tell him you owe him nothing at all. He waits out your shouting the way a mountain waits for weather, then begins his account anyway.

nodes.text: A hovel built against a cottage wall, he says, and a knot-hole to watch through. A blind old man, his son, his daughter. He learned words the way a dog does and then far better — took their language, then their books, then hauled their winter firewood and stacked it at the door before dawn so they would think it luck. Speaking to the blind man went well. Then the family came home.

choices.consequence: You picture the firewood appearing each morning at a stranger's door, and cannot make that picture sit in the same head as the marks on William's throat.
You hunt through it for the lie and find instead the detail no liar bothers inventing: he says the daughter was called Agatha, and then stops talking.

nodes.text: One companion, he says. As deformed and dreadful as himself, so that neither of them is ever looked at again. South America. Acorns and berries. No human eye on either of them for the rest of their lives. He is reasonable all the way through. He quotes Milton at you from memory. Then, in the same reasonable voice, he explains how completely he can ruin you, and you believe every word.

choices.consequence: You give your word on a glacier to a thing you assembled, and he thanks you with real courtesy, which is somehow the worst minute you have had yet.
You say never. He does not argue the point. He simply names your wedding as an occasion he intends to attend.

nodes.text: The Orkneys: three huts, five inhabitants, and a table you carried up from the boat on your own back. She is a spine, a ribcage, and one finished hand so far. You gave her the same wrists. Some nights you sit looking at her and think about children — that they might breed, that a species might come out of this room, and that all of it would be traceable to you.

choices.consequence: Your hands go on working while the rest of you argues. Skill is like that. It has never once required your permission to continue.
You imagine a lineage crossing an ocean, and your fingers have closed on the shears before the thought is even finished.

nodes.text: You take her apart on the table. It is quick; she was mostly promise. When you look up he is at the window with his face pressed flat against the glass, and he has watched all of it. There is no roar. He says he will be with you on your wedding night in the tone of a man confirming a business appointment. Then the window is empty and the sea is very loud.

choices.consequence: You row the pieces out at three in the morning and drop them weighted, then fall asleep in the boat and wake out of sight of any land at all.
You shout his name at the black square of the window until your throat quits. The rain answers. He has already gone off to keep his word.

nodes.text: Irish constables walk you into a shed to view a body they expect will be a stranger to you. It is Henry, who spooned broth into you for five weeks and told your father it was only overwork. Black fingermarks at the throat, the same span as William's. You go down convulsing on the shed floor, and they hold you two months on suspicion of murdering him, which is near enough true.

choices.consequence: You give a fevered account of a creature to a Mr Kirwin, who writes every word down and then sends for a physician rather than a magistrate.
You let them take you for a madman rather than a maker. Your father comes all the way to Ireland to fetch you home, and asks you nothing.

nodes.text: Evian. A room above the lake, shutters latched, a pistol in your coat and a knife under it. He promised to come for you, so you send Elizabeth up alone and walk the corridors like a hired watchman — every closet, both staircases, the servants' passage twice over. In your entire life you have never once misread a sentence put in front of you. You misread this one.

choices.consequence: You stand outside her door with your hand on the latch, hear her humming something, and step away to check the corridor one more time.
You tell yourself it is you he wants, not her. That turns out to be the last comfortable thought available to you.

nodes.text: The sound comes from the room you left her in. She is thrown across the bed, one arm hanging, hair over her face, and there are marks on her neck you have now seen three times on three different people. The window stands open. Out across the moonlit water something enormous is grinning at you from the shoreline. You fire. You miss. It enters the lake and swims.

choices.consequence: You swear on every grave you have filled to hunt him to the Pole, and the vow feels good in your mouth, which tells you something you would rather not know.
You lie down beside her and stay until they lift you off, and learn that grief, in your case, will always smell faintly of lake water.

nodes.text: You carry the news to Geneva yourself and watch it land in his face. He is seventy-two. He gets through the funeral, then four days, and then his arms give out on the arms of his chair and he cannot lift his own head off his chest. On the last afternoon he asks who you are, twice. The house now contains one Frankenstein, and none of it was the house's doing.

choices.consequence: You hold a cup of water to a mouth that has stopped wanting water, and say nothing true, and let him die believing his family was simply unlucky.
You leave the deathbed to check the shutters, because somewhere in you the hunt has already started and the grieving will have to be fitted in later.

nodes.text: North, past the last settlement with a name on any chart. You buy a sledge and six dogs with what remains of the family money and follow a track no man could leave: the strides too long, the abandoned fires still warm to the back of your hand. Once he leaves a heap of frozen meat where you cannot miss it. He is feeding you. He wants this to go on.

choices.consequence: You cut the frozen meat with your teeth and drive the dogs harder, understanding as you chew that being kept alive by someone is a form of being owned.
You sit on the sledge in the whiteness and count what lies behind you: five graves, no wife, no father, no work. There is nothing left to turn back toward.

nodes.text: The ice takes the ship at seventy-eight degrees north and holds it like a fist. At dawn a sailor points: a sledge out on a floe, one dog alive of six, and a man on it who will not come aboard until he has been told which direction the ship intends to sail. Captain Walton gives up his own cabin for you. He is twenty-eight. Nobody has ever listened to you like this.

choices.consequence: You talk for a week while he takes it down in letters to his sister, and it is the first time the thing has existed anywhere outside your own skull.
You keep it behind your teeth three days. Then he describes what he would sacrifice for glory, and you begin at the garret and the rain.

nodes.text: Your lungs are finished and the surgeon has stopped coming by. The crew are at the cabin door demanding the ship turn south, and Walton keeps glancing at you to settle it. You get up on one elbow and give them a speech about glory that would shame a general — men made for honour, not for retreat — and they cheer, and you drop back on the pillow, appalled at yourself.

choices.consequence: You take back every word of that speech in a whisper meant only for him, and tell him a small quiet life does not count as a defeat.

choices.text: Ask him to kill the creature
choices.consequence: You make him swear it with your fist in his cuff, and see plainly in his face that he is only agreeing to soothe a dying man.

nodes.text: Nine in the evening, and the cabin lamp swings with the working of the floe. You go through the arithmetic one final time — William, Justine, Henry, Elizabeth, your father — and cannot locate the step where you did wrong, only the long stretch where you did not stop. Walton is still writing. The pen keeps moving for a while after you stop talking, and then it stops as well.

choices.consequence: Your fingers close around a near-stranger's and he lets them, so you die being touched by somebody, which is more than you ever arranged for anyone else.
You turn your face to the porthole and the ice past it, still watching for movement out there, still hunting with the last minute you have.

nodes.text: At midnight Walton hears something in the cabin and finds him bent over the berth, one enormous hand held above your face without touching it, making a sound the captain has no word for. He says he came asking for sympathy and was given a manhunt. He says the murders sickened him while his own hands were doing them. He asks the pardon of a dead man who is in no position to grant it.

choices.consequence: The captain stands frozen in the doorway and lets the thing finish, and every word goes into the letters, which is precisely how it outlives you.
You are past hearing any of it. Whatever he needed to say to you arrives eight hours late, in a room with a swinging lamp.

nodes.text: He will go north, he says, to the farthest ice, build a fire out of whatever will burn, and climb onto it himself. The wind will take the ash out over a sea nobody sails. He says he will exult in the agony — then, much more quietly, that no one will mourn him, because no one exists who could. He steps through the port onto a raft of ice, and the dark has him inside a minute.

choices.consequence: Walton watches the floe until the lamp gutters out, then writes that the creature was borne away and lost in the distance. He intends that as a conclusion.
Nothing is ever recovered — no fire, no ash, no bones on any floe anyone charts. Certain deaths only occur if you agree to stop looking for the body.

nodes.text: In England, Margaret Saville will receive a packet of her brother's letters about ice, ambition, and a dead man's confession. Below deck the crew are already breaking out the ice-saws. Walton has his own arithmetic to work: a passage to the Pole, or the twenty men who signed articles with him. He has just spent a week watching what becomes of a man who chooses the discovery.

choices.consequence: One ship turns south with every hand still breathing, which makes it the only decision anywhere in this account that costs nobody anything.
Some part of you still wants the Pole reached, by anybody, at any price at all. It is the same part that lit the second candle in the garret.
You stop watching the captain and look north instead, out at the empty ice, where a thing that can quote Milton is walking away from all of it alive.

nodes.text: He goes north until the ice will not carry a raft, and there he builds his fire from driftwood, sledge runners, and the boards that brought him. The last of your work burns with the last of him. Walton's ship turns south with every man aboard still living. You are buried at sea in canvas with two roundshot at your feet, and the ocean keeps no record of the name, though everyone else will.

He writes it down honestly, including the parts that make him look small: the ambition, the mutinous crew, the hour he sat crying in a cold cabin. The packet reaches his sister, and she keeps it, and it is copied, and copied again. Two centuries on, a boy in a lit room reads about a creature learning language through a hole in a wall, and quietly takes his side.

No fire is ever found. Whalers pass a story around about an island with cairns on it and marks worked into the flat stones — charcoal, a careful hand, the letters far too large. He is setting down what happened to him, in order, with every name spelled correctly. He has read enough by now to know that whoever writes it down is the one who ends up believed.
